e.etymology: A pet form of Edith, from Old English Eadgyth, built from ead, wealth or fortune, and gyth, war. It is also given as a full name.
namesakes: Edie Falco (star of The Sopranos and Nurse Jackie)
Edie Sedgwick (1960s model and Andy Warhol muse)
Edie Brickell (singer-songwriter)

e.etymology: From Arabic jannah, garden, the Quran's word for paradise. Muslim families in English-speaking countries have taken it up as a girls' name.

assoc.t: Jannah, ex-stormtrooper in The Rise of Skywalker

e.etymology: A respelling of Braxton, an English surname from a place name, Old English for the settlement of a man called Bracca. The -yn ending follows names such as Jordyn and Paxtyn.
From the Irish surname O Ruanaidh, descendant of Ruanaidh, a byname meaning champion. Actress Rooney Mara, who goes by her middle name, brought it into use for girls.
namesakes: Rooney Mara (star of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo)

assoc.t: Mickey Rooney, classic Hollywood actor (surname)
Wayne Rooney, English soccer star (surname)
the NFL's Rooney Rule, named for the Steelers' owner

e.etymology: A modern Indian girls' name that became popular with Hindu families in India and abroad in the 2010s. Its Sanskrit source is not firmly documented.
The Spanish and Italian form of Eloise, French Heloise, usually traced to the Germanic name Helewidis, from words for hale and wide. Heloise was the learned 12th-century abbess who loved Abelard.
Not a chosen name. Social Security birth records use Unknown as a placeholder when a baby's first name was not recorded.
e.note: A records placeholder, not a real given name; it appears in the data because some births were filed without a first name.

e.etymology: A spelling of Hakeem, from Arabic hakim, wise. Basketball star Hakeem Olajuwon was known as Akeem early in his career, and Eddie Murphy played Prince Akeem in Coming to America (1988).
namesakes: Hakeem Olajuwon (NBA Hall of Famer, known as Akeem until 1991)

assoc.t: Prince Akeem, Eddie Murphy in Coming to America

e.etymology: A 21st-century spelling of Ava that writes out the long A. Ava is usually taken as a form of Eve, Hebrew for life, and was also a medieval Germanic name of uncertain meaning.
The usual spelling of Clara in German, Scandinavian and Slavic languages, from Latin clara, bright, clear or famous. Saint Clare of Assisi, the 13th-century follower of Francis, spread the name.
namesakes: Klara (robot narrator of Ishiguro's novel Klara and the Sun)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Aiden favored by Spanish-speaking families in the United States. Aiden is from Irish Aodhan, a pet form of Aodh, fire.

The German, Scandinavian and Polish spelling of Oscar. Oscar comes from Irish legend, where it is read as deer friend, or from Old English Osgar, god's spear; it spread across Europe through the Ossian poems of the 1760s.
namesakes: Oskar Schindler (German industrialist of Schindler's List)

assoc.t: the Oscars, Hollywood's Academy Awards (same sound)

e.etymology: From the English word serene and a rare variant of Serena, both from Latin serenus, calm and clear. Arab families also use this spelling for the name Sirin.
A pet form of Benjamin, from Hebrew Binyamin, usually read as son of the right hand. American use as a full name jumped after the 1974 dog movie Benji.
namesakes: Benji Madden (Good Charlotte guitarist)

assoc.t: Benji, the stray dog hero of the 1970s films

e.etymology: From Old French Gui, a Frankish short form of names beginning with widu, wood. The Normans brought it to England. In Israel Guy is a separate name, from Hebrew gai, valley.
namesakes: Guy Fieri (Food Network host)
Guy Ritchie (film director)
Guy Fawkes (Gunpowder Plot conspirator)

assoc.t: guy, the everyday word for a man
Guy Fieri, Food Network host
Guy Fawkes of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot

e.note: Guy is the everyday word for a man, which itself comes from Guy Fawkes, so the name can get lost in conversation.

e.etymology: A surname used as a first name, often a short form of McCoy, from Irish Mac Aodha, son of Aodh. It matches the English word coy, shy or reserved, and was most used in the early 1900s.

assoc.t: coy, meaning shy or playfully evasive
koi, the ornamental pond carp (same sound)

e.etymology: A modern American name, a spelling in the family of Ayanna, Aiyana and Iyana. The source of those names is debated and no single meaning is established.
From Hebrew Ovadyah, from oved, servant or worshipper, and Yah, a name of God. Obadiah is the prophet whose one-chapter book is the shortest in the Old Testament.
namesakes: Obadiah (Old Testament prophet)
Obadiah Stane (villain of the first Iron Man film)

e.etymology: A less common spelling of Frederick, the English form of German Friedrich, from Germanic words for peace and for king or ruler.
From an English surname, a medieval nickname from Middle English trewe, faithful, and man. Use as a first name peaked in 1945, the year Harry S. Truman became president.
namesakes: Truman Capote (author of In Cold Blood)
Truman Burbank (Jim Carrey's role in The Truman Show)

assoc.t: Harry S. Truman, 33rd US president (surname)
The Truman Show, 1998 Jim Carrey film

e.etymology: From the title baron, the lowest rank of the British peerage, which came into English from Old French. Baron is also a surname in many European languages.
namesakes: Baron Davis (NBA All-Star guard)

assoc.t: baron, a rank of nobility
Barron Trump, Donald Trump's youngest son (same sound)

e.note: Sounds the same as the word barren.

e.etymology: From the state. Its name is uncertain, probably from O'odham ali sonak, small spring, by way of Spanish, or possibly from Basque haritz ona, good oak. It was given to American girls around 1900.
namesakes: Arizona Robbins (surgeon on Grey's Anatomy)

assoc.t: Arizona, the southwestern US state
AriZona iced tea
USS Arizona, battleship sunk at Pearl Harbor
Arizona Cardinals, Diamondbacks and Wildcats teams

e.etymology: A pet form of Mildred, Millicent, Emily and Camilla that is also given as a full name. Millie is the more common spelling.

assoc.t: the Milly Rock, a hip-hop dance move

e.etymology: A modern American name in the family of Amara, Amari and Mariah, with no single documented source. It also resembles Amariah, a biblical men's name.

e.meaning: great house; title of Egypt's kings
e.etymology: From the title of the kings of ancient Egypt, Egyptian per-aa, great house, first the palace and later the ruler. It reached English through Hebrew, Greek and Latin in the Bible.

assoc.t: pharaoh, title of ancient Egypt's rulers

e.note: A royal title used as a name; in the Bible Pharaoh is the ruler who enslaves the Israelites in Exodus.

e.etymology: A respelling of Blakely with the -leigh ending. Blakely is an English surname and place name from Old English words for dark or black and for a woodland clearing.

e.meaning: from Cynthia, of Mount Cynthus, or Lucinda, light
e.etymology: A short form of Lucinda and Cinderella that the 20th century adopted as the pet form of Cynthia, a Greek title of the goddess Artemis. It was a top-100 American name from the 1950s into the 1970s.
namesakes: Cindy Crawford (supermodel)
Cindy Lou Who (the little girl in How the Grinch Stole Christmas)
Cindy Brady (youngest daughter on The Brady Bunch)

e.meaning: gift of God (as a pet form of Dorothy)
e.etymology: A pet form of Dorothy, from Greek Dorothea, gift of God, and also of Dolores and Doris. The word doll for a toy comes from this nickname.
namesakes: Dolly Parton (country music legend)
Dolley Madison (first lady, wife of James Madison)

assoc.t: Dolly Parton, country music legend
Dolly the sheep, first cloned mammal (1996)
Hello, Dolly!, the Broadway musical
dolly, a child's doll or a wheeled cart

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Raghallaigh, descendant of Raghallach, an old personal name of uncertain meaning. Riley is the commoner spelling as a first name.

e.meaning: supplanter (as a short form of Jacob)
e.etymology: A pet form of Jacob, from Hebrew Ya'akov, traditionally read as holder of the heel or supplanter. In Dutch Coby is a woman's name, short for Jacoba.
namesakes: Coby White (NBA guard)

assoc.t: Kobe Bryant, NBA legend (same sound)

e.etymology: From the river Nile, whose name reached English through Latin Nilus and Greek Neilos; the Greek word's own source is unknown. It is also used as a form of Niles.
namesakes: Nile Rodgers (Chic guitarist and record producer)

assoc.t: the Nile, the great river of Egypt and East Africa

e.etymology: An American variant of Brianna, the feminine of Brian, an Irish name probably from a Celtic root meaning high or noble. The Bre- spelling follows the nickname Bree.
namesakes: Breanna Stewart (WNBA MVP and Olympic gold medalist)
